Pregnancy

Blurred vision in pregnancy: eye changes and when to get help

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pregnancy can affect how your eyes focus and how comfortable they feel. Some changes are temporary, but new blurred vision cannot safely be labelled hormonal without assessment. Contact your maternity team immediately about a new visual disturbance; sudden sight loss or other emergency symptoms need emergency care. An eye examination can help distinguish a prescription or tear-film change from a problem needing treatment.

What a change in vision can mean

Blurred vision means that an image is less clear; double vision, flashing lights, missing areas or distorted lines are different symptoms. Tell the clinician exactly what has changed, whether it affects one or both eyes, when it began and whether it comes and goes. A symptom disappearing does not always make it harmless.

There is no single reliable percentage that predicts how likely a particular pregnancy is to cause blur. Studies measure different changes in different groups. Neither being early in pregnancy nor having normal vision before conception rules out a problem. The aim is to identify the cause, not to reassure from a population statistic.

Hormones, fluid and the focusing surface

Hormonal and fluid changes can alter the tear film and the cornea, the clear front surface of the eye. Changes in corneal thickness or curvature may temporarily change refraction: how light is focused. Research findings vary, and not everyone experiences a measurable prescription change.

These effects may occur at different points in pregnancy and sometimes continue during breastfeeding. They do not explain every new symptom. A clinician checks whether the change fits a temporary focusing problem or whether the retina, optic nerve, blood pressure or another cause needs attention.

Dryness and contact-lens discomfort

An unstable tear film can cause grittiness, burning, watering or fluctuating blur. Pregnancy-related changes may contribute, but screens, airflow, eyelid problems and medicines can also matter. Improvement after blinking or removing lenses is useful information, not proof that no other assessment is needed.

If lenses are uncomfortable, remove them and use glasses while obtaining advice. Pregnancy alone does not forbid contact lenses, but the fit, prescription or wearing schedule may need review. A red eye in a contact-lens wearer, or a painful red eye, needs urgent assessment rather than continued lens wear.

Glasses, daily tasks and elective eye surgery

A small temporary change may not need new glasses, and a definitive prescription may be rechecked once vision stabilizes after pregnancy. However, do not postpone an examination or struggle with unsafe vision because you were told that glasses must never change during pregnancy. Discuss reading, work and driving difficulties; the eye-care professional can judge whether an interim correction is useful.

Avoid driving whenever your vision is not clear enough to do so safely. Ask someone else to take you for urgent care. Elective laser refractive surgery such as LASIK is generally deferred during pregnancy and breastfeeding because measurements can fluctuate; its timing is a separate decision from getting necessary vision care.

Migraine and feeling faint

Migraine aura can cause temporary zigzags, lights or a blind spot, sometimes with little headache. A new or changed visual episode in pregnancy must not be self-diagnosed as migraine. Seek immediate maternity advice; sudden severe headache, serious visual loss, new weakness, speech difficulty, confusion or a seizure needs emergency assessment.

Standing up quickly can make someone feel faint during pregnancy. Sit down, or lie on your side if needed, and rise slowly. Report episodes that recur or do not settle, and describe any visual symptoms. Rest, hydration or a dark room may help an assessed benign problem, but should not delay investigation of new visual disturbance.

Blood pressure and pre-eclampsia

Pre-eclampsia is an important cause to rule out when vision changes in pregnancy or after birth. It most often develops from 20 weeks, but symptoms should be assessed whatever the gestation. Blurring or flashing lights can occur with it; severe headache, pain below the ribs, vomiting, sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet, heartburn that does not improve with heartburn medicine, or feeling very unwell are other warnings. Any one warrants immediate maternity contact; do not wait for several signs together or a home blood-pressure result.

Diagnosis uses clinical assessment, blood pressure, urine and sometimes blood tests and fetal checks. Eye symptoms alone cannot confirm or grade the condition. Treatment and birth timing depend on the findings; bed rest is not a substitute for care. HELLP syndrome and seizures are serious related complications, and monitoring may still be needed after delivery.

Blood glucose and diabetic eye disease

High glucose can temporarily affect the eye tissues involved in focusing, but blur does not diagnose gestational diabetes or prove that glucose is the only cause. Follow the maternity team’s testing and treatment plan, and have new vision changes assessed even if a glucose reading looks acceptable.

Pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes can increase the risk of retinopathy worsening during pregnancy, so planned eye checks matter. Gestational diabetes alone does not usually lead to diabetic retinopathy during that pregnancy; routine screening policies therefore differ. For example, England offers pregnancy retinal screening for pre-existing diabetes, not gestational diabetes alone. This screening distinction never means ignoring symptoms.

Retinal, optic-nerve and visual-field problems

A new curtain or shadow, a missing area, new or increased floaters, flashes, or wavy central vision needs immediate eye assessment. Retinal fluid leakage, detachment or other retinal disorders are among the possible causes. Sudden inability to see from one or both eyes is an emergency, even without pain.

Optic neuritis is inflammation of the optic nerve; it may affect clarity, colour or the visual field and cause pain with eye movement. Papilloedema is optic-disc swelling related to raised pressure around the brain. Neither is a normal cosmetic pregnancy change. Loss of side vision should not be dismissed as ordinary pituitary growth; mention any known pituitary disorder. Darkening of the skin around the eyes is different from dark areas inside your vision.

What an assessment may involve

The team may check visual acuity, the glasses prescription, pupils, colour and visual fields, the eye surface and the back of the eye, depending on symptoms. Blood pressure or glucose assessment may be needed alongside eye care. Tell every clinician that you are pregnant or breastfeeding and list medicines, eye drops and previous eye conditions.

Pregnancy is not a reason to avoid an indicated eye examination. Dilated retinal examinations are used in pregnancy when needed, including diabetic screening. The clinician chooses tests and treatment for the situation and explains any precautions. Drops used for an examination may temporarily blur vision; arrange suitable transport and follow the service’s advice.

Comfort measures after the cause is assessed

For an assessed tear-film or eye-strain problem, take screen breaks, blink regularly and reduce direct airflow. Glasses may be more comfortable than lenses. Rest can ease discomfort, but is not treatment for unexplained loss of vision or a substitute for checking a new symptom.

Ask a pharmacist or eye-care professional to check the exact lubricant product for pregnancy and lens use. Carmellose sodium is one lubricant that NHS guidance considers suitable in pregnancy and breastfeeding; this does not mean every medicated or redness-relief drop is interchangeable. Follow the product instructions and do not stop prescribed eye treatment without advice.

What to expect after birth

Some temporary focusing and tear-film changes settle after delivery, while others take longer or persist during breastfeeding. There is no promise that vision returns immediately or completely to its previous state. Arrange the recommended recheck, especially if glasses no longer work well or symptoms affect daily activities.

New or worsening visual disturbance after birth still needs immediate advice; postpartum pre-eclampsia and eye disease are not excluded by having delivered. Do not wait for weaning to investigate persistent or concerning symptoms. If you have diabetes, retinopathy or another eye disorder, continue the follow-up plan rather than assuming birth ends the risk.

Know which service to contact

Contact maternity care immediately for a new visual disturbance during pregnancy or in the weeks after birth. Obtain immediate eye assessment for new flashes or floaters, a curtain or shadow, a missing field area or distorted central vision; tell the maternity team as well. Do not wait for a routine appointment.

An eye that is very dark red, an eye injury or puncture, or something stuck in the eye also warrants emergency care on its own. Seek emergency care for sudden sight loss, sudden severe eye pain, pain when looking at light, a red eye with severe headache and nausea, or a sudden extremely severe headache. Call emergency services for new face or limb weakness, speech difficulty, confusion or a seizure, even if stroke-like symptoms stop. Do not drive yourself or wait for several warning signs to appear.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Report new visual symptoms promptly and describe their onset, pattern and effect on daily life.

Have focusing changes assessed alongside possible obstetric, glucose, retinal or optic-nerve causes.

Individualize correction, treatment and postpartum follow-up with the appropriate clinical team.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help keep symptom descriptions, medicines and appointment questions together. It cannot examine the eyes, diagnose the cause of blur or monitor an emergency; recording information must not delay care.

When to seek help

Contact maternity care immediately for new visual disturbance during pregnancy or after birth. New flashes, floaters, shadows or central distortion need immediate eye advice. Sudden sight loss, sudden severe eye pain, pain when looking at light, a red eye with severe headache and nausea, or a sudden extremely severe headache needs emergency care. New weakness, speech difficulty, confusion or a seizure requires emergency services, even if stroke-like symptoms stop. Do not drive yourself.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Temporary focusing changes are possible, but new blur requires assessment rather than automatic reassurance.
  • Discuss glasses and contact-lens needs with an eye-care professional; necessary examination should not wait until after birth.
  • Pregnancy blood-pressure problems, glucose changes and eye disease require different assessments.
  • Visual-field loss, new flashes or floaters, distortion, eye pain and sudden sight loss must not be treated as ordinary hormonal symptoms.
  • Keep follow-up after birth and during breastfeeding if symptoms persist or an eye condition is being monitored.

Frequently asked questions

Is blurred vision in pregnancy always dangerous?

No, but its cause cannot be judged safely from pregnancy alone. Temporary focusing or tear-film changes can occur. Contact maternity care immediately about a new visual disturbance and follow advice for eye assessment; emergency signs need emergency care.

Will it disappear as soon as the baby is born?

Not necessarily. Some changes settle after birth, others take longer or persist during breastfeeding, and an underlying eye problem may need treatment. New or worsening symptoms after birth still need immediate assessment.

Can a swollen cornea change my prescription?

Fluid-related changes in the cornea may alter focusing or lens comfort, but findings vary. An eye examination helps determine whether refraction is the cause and whether a temporary correction or later recheck is appropriate.

Can pregnancy cause dry eyes?

Pregnancy may contribute to tear-film changes, but dryness also has other causes. Use glasses if lenses are uncomfortable and ask about an appropriate lubricant. Do not assume that significant new blur, pain or a red contact-lens eye is simple dryness.

Should I wait until after pregnancy to get glasses checked?

Do not delay a necessary examination or tolerate unsafe vision. A final prescription may be rechecked when vision stabilizes, but an eye-care professional can help with current functional needs. Elective laser surgery is a separate matter and is generally deferred.

Does blurred vision mean I have gestational diabetes?

No. Glucose changes can affect focusing, but many other causes exist. Follow recommended diabetes testing and seek assessment of new symptoms. Pre-existing diabetes and gestational diabetes have different routine retinal-screening needs.

Can I use eye drops while pregnant?

Some lubricants, such as carmellose sodium, are suitable, but check the exact product and lens instructions with a pharmacist or eye-care professional. Do not start an unknown medicated drop or stop prescribed treatment on your own.

Which symptoms need emergency care?

Sudden sight loss, sudden severe eye pain, pain when looking at light, a red eye with severe headache and nausea, or a sudden extremely severe headache needs emergency care. Call emergency services for new weakness, speech difficulty, confusion or a seizure, even if stroke-like symptoms stop. Do not drive yourself. Other new visual symptoms still require immediate maternity or eye advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
